data.title: Moravany nad Váhom – Hradište, a fortified hilltop above the Váh
data.excerpt: Moravany nad Váhom in the Piešťany district is known above all for mammoth remains and for the Palaeolithic Venus carved from mammoth ivory, dated to 22,800 years BC. Above the village, the locality known as Hradište carries a fortification of the 12th–13th centuries, while a pre-Great Moravian spur and an iron stylus of the 9th century show that the crossing over the Považský Inovec mattered much earlier.
data.metaTitle: Moravany nad Váhom – Hradište and the ivory Venus
data.metaDescription: Moravany nad Váhom, famed for the Venus of mammoth ivory, also has the fortified Hradište locality, a pre-Great Moravian spur and a 9th-century iron stylus.

children.text: Moravany nad Váhom (Piešťany district) is known above all for the finds of mammoth remains and for the occupation of the Palaeolithic period. Among the most important finds coming from the cadastral area of the village is the figurine of a Venus made of mammoth ivory, which is assigned to the Gravettian culture (22,800 years BC).

Surface collection and systematic archaeological excavation in the cadastral area of the village have also identified finds and occupation of the Neolithic and the Eneolithic, the Final Bronze Age, the Early and Late Iron Age and the Late Roman period. From the surroundings of the village we know of occupation of the 9th–10th centuries at the locality known as Kostolec at Ducové, in the villages of Hubina and Banka, and from the fortified localities of Hradište and Marhát.

Several scholars have devoted attention to place names of the Moravany–Moravce type, most often explaining the name as 1. places of settlers resettled from Moravia, 2. important communication points in the Great Moravian period, 3. in the Váh region, as the seat of Mojmír's retinues stationed in the territory of the former principality of Pribina, with the task of pacifying the country.

The fortified locality of Hradište attracted the attention of the doyen of Slovak archaeology, Štefan Janšák, who surveyed it. In a short article in 1930 he states that it lies 3 km east of the village of Moravany as spot height 371 of a side ridge of the Hlohovec hills, falling away into the valley of the Stríbernica brook, a small tributary of the Váh. The ridge mentioned and the south-western valley adjoining it bear the name “Hradište”. A small plateau, 50 m long and 30 m wide, lying on a naturally widened part of the ridge, is protected on the southern and northern sides by a steep slope, and in the direction of the axis of the ridge, on the eastern and western sides, by short ramparts c d, e f about 1 m high. In 1973 a trial archaeological excavation was carried out at this locality, followed by its evaluation (Ruttkay 1975, 1989).

The prehistoric occupation of the Final Bronze Age and of the Early and Late Iron Age at this locality was disturbed and partly destroyed in the Middle Ages. At that time the upper plateau was levelled, a ditch was built below the acropolis and a low rampart on its outer side. The upper plateau was encircled by a rampart with a core of drystone-laid stones covered with a clay mantle. On the western, lower-lying plateau the ground plans of two rectangular log buildings with ovens were recognised, together with a pit of oval plan – a cistern (?). On the basis of distinctive associated material the hilltop fortification was dated to the 12th–13th centuries.

children.text: Among the interesting finds from this site is an iron knife dated to the Late Iron Age – the La Tène culture – as well as a knife, a ring, a star-shaped rowel from a spur, a small chisel (?), a cramp and others, broadly dated to the 13th century. Part of the sherds collected belongs to the period of the Final Bronze Age – the Lusatian culture. The sherd material, predominantly from pot-shaped vessels and thick-walled storage vessels decorated with an incised multiple line, with stab marks and with wavy lines, is dated to the 13th century. Among the interesting finds is a fragment of a flask-shaped vessel decorated with incised wavy lines.

Early medieval finds of the pre-Great Moravian and Great Moravian periods are represented from the village by the find of an iron stylus (9th century AD) from the locality known as Lopata and by a pre-Great Moravian spur. The iron stylus (length 135 mm) has a flatly hammered triangular head and a long shank. The head is pointed on both sides by forging, which testifies to its functional use – smoothing out the written text on wax tablets. In Slovakia this is so far the first example of its kind; in Moravia there are 14 of them to date, of which 9 come from Mikulčice-Valy and 5 from Uherské Hradiště-Sady. R. Bača links the find of the stylus with the nearby hillfort at Ducové, and considers the possibility that it reached Moravany in connection with the expulsion of Methodius's disciples from Great Moravia. The discovery of further early medieval artefacts from Moravany and the most recent research at Bojná and its surroundings, however, also make it possible to consider that the stylus was used directly at Moravany.

children.text: From the period before the rise of Great Moravia comes the find of an iron spur from the locality known as Hradište (369 m above sea level), from a spot about 170 m east of the summit. The spur was found by chance in 2000, having been pushed to the surface of the ground by a tree root. Today it is kept in a private collection. This type of spur is not so very common. In Slovakia a spur with eyelets was found at the early medieval hillfort at Pobedim in the pre-Great Moravian horizon beneath the destruction of the rampart, and it is dated to the 8th century. Two spurs with eyelets come from the hillfort at Smolenice-Molpír as well. One of the spurs from Smolenice-Molpír has its arms decorated on the outer sides with straight grooving, while the spur from Moravany nad Váhom has them decorated on the outer side with oblique grooving. Iron spurs with arms ending in an oval eyelet curved inwards, with a short conical point at the apex, were also found at Čakajovce.

children.text: It is probable that such spurs reached the Slavic pre-Great Moravian milieu from the territory of Germany. According to the classification of D. Bialeková, the spur from Moravany nad Váhom can be assigned to type IIA (Bialeková 1977). Finds of spurs are often linked to fortified centres, and the place where they occur may be regarded as important for the period concerned. From the end of the 7th century and during the 8th century the Slavic settlement substratum became stabilised in the territory of Slovakia (north of the Avar Khaganate), while in the second half of the 8th and at the beginning of the 9th century conditions gradually arose for the subsequent emergence of the Principality of Nitra. It is possible that the locality known as Hradište at Moravany nad Váhom, occupied already in prehistory and with a fortification of the 12th–13th centuries, had strategic importance in the pre-Great Moravian period as well. In this connection a relationship to the surrounding early medieval sites (e.g. Banka, Bašovce, Bojná, Ducové and Pobedim) may also be considered.

children.text: A. Ruttkay regards the small hilltop castle at the locality known as Hradište as part of the castle estate of Tematín. The first written report of this castle, which arose on royal initiative, dates from 1270. The fortified locality was connected with the administration of the royal treasury in controlling the communication crossings over the Považský Inovec mountains in this area. The fortification evidently had a similar function also in the period of Great Moravia, above all in connection with the older fortifications of the 9th–10th centuries lining the ancient crossing to the Váh region and on to Moravia, with the central hillfort at the locality known as Valy in the cadastral area of the village of Bojná.
